title: Holy Week's middle days
hookLine: Monday to Wednesday: the fig tree, the temple, the anointing

lines: A TREE, A TABLE, A JAR.
cards: So what happened on the Monday? Between the shouting on the road and the supper on Thursday are a few days that are easy to skip. Mark sets three strange scenes among them.

A fig tree covered in leaves and bare of fruit. Tables tipped over in the temple courts, coins rolling on the stones. And a dinner in Bethany where a woman breaks open a jar of perfume and pours it over Jesus's head.
Tradition spreads these scenes across the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of Holy Week: the held breath before everything happens.

teach.h: A TREE ALL LEAVES, NO FRUIT.
teach.b: First, the tree. Jesus is hungry, sees a fig tree in leaf, and finds nothing on it; Mark even adds that it wasn't the season for figs. Jesus speaks to it, and the next morning it has withered from the roots.
Notice where Mark puts it: the tree comes before the temple scene and the withering after, so each frames the other.
Some readers hear in it a warning about any religious life, their own included, that's all leaves and no fruit. Second, the temple.
Jesus drives out the people buying and selling and overturns the money tables, quoting the prophets of Israel.

teach.h: A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL NATIONS.
teach.b: In the King James: "Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves." Of all nations.
Some readers hear him defending the temple's own calling, in the words of its own scriptures. Third, the jar. At a dinner in Bethany, a woman breaks an alabaster jar of costly ointment over his head.
Some at the table are indignant: what a waste.

teach.h: SHE HATH DONE WHAT SHE COULD.
teach.b: Jesus says, let her alone, and then: "She hath done what she could: she is come aforehand to anoint my body to the burying." A burial anointing, ahead of time.
Right after, Mark says, Judas goes to the chief priests, which is why some places call Wednesday Spy Wednesday.
Three quiet scenes. A tree that says nothing. A courtyard cleared.

how: Some churches hold daily services on the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of Holy Week, reading the Gospel scenes of these days; some households use them to clean and prepare for Easter.

games.q: you're at the dinner in Bethany. a woman breaks a jar of costly ointment and pours it on his head. people mutter about the waste. what does Jesus say?
o: it should have been sold instead.
let her alone. she hath done what she could.
games.why: he defends her: she has anointed his body ahead of time for burying.

practice: Tidy one corner of the room you're in, slowly: pick up what's on the floor, straighten what's crooked. The temple was cleared and the dinner room filled with something costly; either way, a space got ready for what was coming.
If you pray, do it in silence as an offering; if not, notice how the room changes when there's room in it.

wordCard.voice: Alabaster. The jar of costly ointment a woman broke open over Jesus's head at Bethany, one of three quiet scenes in Holy Week's middle days.

orig.note: Greek: an alabaster jar, the one the woman breaks open in Mark 14:3.

carryVoice: Your line: the quiet before. From Patrick's breastplate and Joseph's silence, through Mary's yes and going home, to an opened tomb and a road of branches: that was the week. See you tomorrow.
